newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt suffers setback with STET vote.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt suffers setback with STET vote.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government suffered a serious setback on Wednesday when the lower house narrowly voted against a plan to transfer control of telecommunications giant STET to the Treasury.
The government lost on the decree concerning the tranfer from state holdings giant IRI with a vote of 230 for, 234 against, and 26 abstentions.
Some 140 parliamentarians were not present for the vote.

The government was defeated after the hard-left Communist Refoundation, which guarantees Prodi's majority in the lower house, abstained and centre-right oppostion parties mustered enough votes to deliever the shock defeat.
Commmnist Refoundation is ideologically opposed to the STET privatisation.
The Treasury said the vote would not sink the transfer plan because it was attached to part of the 1997 budget and effectively had "already taken place."
The government would provide "appropriate solutions" to complete those aspects of the plan that were regulated by the decree that was rejected by parliament, the Treasury said.
But the damage to the coalition appeared clear.
"This was a real misfortune," said Labour Minister Tiziano Treu.
Massimo D'Alema, head of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), the largest party in Prime Minister Romano Prodi's coalition, said the vote was a very serious setback.
D'Alema hoped that the government could seek a remedy.
Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco said the vote was "uninfluential" because the tranfer was already in the 1997 budget. "There should be no negative consequences on the markets," he said.
But some analysts said they feared negative repercussions on the Milan bourse on Thursday following a week of strong gains.

The oppostion centre-right headed by former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi crowed victory, repeating accusations that Communist Refoundation, which has no ministers in the government, is holding the coalition hostage.
"The government deserved this defeat," said Pietro Armani of the hard-right National Alliance.
Communist Refoundation leaders said they had warned the government they would abstain.
The government last year decided to take STET into the treasury fold ahead of its privatisation, which is slated for later this year.
The transfer allows the government to reduce IRI debt in accordance with a European Union deal.
Under a 1993 accord with the European Union, IRI must cut its debt to below five trillion lire by the end of the year from its end-1995 level of 22.5 trillion.
The Treasury said last month it would pay at least 14.53 trillion lire ($9.3 billion) to debt-laden IRI to take over its controlling stake in STET.
The transfer of shares from IRI to the Treasury was outlined in November when Italy abruptly announced that the privatisation of STET would not go ahead in 1996 as had been planned.
IRI holds 61.27 percent of ordinary shares in STET, Europe's fourth-biggest phone company.
STET acts as a telecommunications holding and in turn controls Telecom Italia, the operating unit. The government is currently working on plans to fuse STET with Telecom Italia.
